```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
library(RColorBrewer)
library(factoextra)
library(mclust)
library(cluster)
```

## The data

Dataset: cancer cell line microarray data.

```{r}
# Load the data
load(file="/Users/dsesia/Desktop/Teaching/Clustering/data.RData")
load(file="/Users/dsesia/Desktop/Teaching/Clustering/labs.RData")
```

```{r}
dim(data)
```

The dataset contains `r nrow(data)` observations and `r ncol(data)` variables (genes). $x_{i,j}$ is the entry of the matrix at line $i$ and column $j$ and it represents the gene $j$ expression in sample $i$.

The data look like this:

```{r}
data[1:4,1:6]
```

For our analysis we will consider the most variable genes and then we will normalize the data:

* Select the 50 most variable genes 
* Scale the data by using the R function <span style="color:blue">scale()</span>. This function is used to scale the columns of a numeric matrix. In particular each entry $x_{i,j}$ of column $X_i$ is transformed in the following way: $x_{i,j}^{\text{scaled}}=\frac{x_{i,j} - \text{mean}(X_i)}{\text{sd}(X_i)}$

```{r}
var=apply(data,2,function(x) var(x,na.rm = TRUE))
var=var[order(var,decreasing = TRUE)]
more.var=names(var)[1:50]
data.var=data[,more.var]
data.var=scale(data.var) #
```

For every sample we also know its cancer type. This information is contained in the vector "labs". 

```{r}
labs
```

In particular, there are 4 different types of cancer: COLON, LEUKEMIA, MELANOMA and NSCLC (Non-Small Cells Lung Cancer). \
We can see how many samples there are for each type by using the R function <span style="color:blue">table()</span>.

```{r}
table(labs)
```

This information is our ground truth, we will consider it for evaluating and comparing different clusters algorithms. 

## Distance matrix

In order to perform clustering on our data, we first need to compute a **distance matrix**. We can do that by using the function <span style="color:blue">dist()</span> (package "stats"). Note that the default distance measure is the euclidean. We can change it by specifying the method that we prefer (ex: "euclidean", "maximum", "manhattan", "binary", ...).

```{r}
dist.matrix=dist(data.var)
as.matrix(dist.matrix)[1:5,1:5]
```

We can visualize our distance matrix with a heatmap:

```{r,out.width="50%"}
# color palette 
col <- colorRampPalette(brewer.pal(9, "GnBu"))(50)

# assign each cancer type a color
temp <- as.numeric(as.factor(labs))
colsamples <- brewer.pal(4, "PiYG")[temp]

heatmap(as.matrix(dist.matrix),Colv = NA, Rowv = NA,col=col,RowSideColors=colsamples,ColSideColors=colsamples)
legend(x="right",legend=c("COLON","LEUKEMIA","MELANOMA","NSCLC"), 
     fill=brewer.pal(4, "PiYG"),cex=0.5)
```

## DBSCAN

The clustering algorithm DBSCAN can be run in R with the function <span style="color:blue">dbscan()</span> (package "dbscan")

```{r}
library(dbscan)
```

*Remark*: DBSCAN requires two input parameters: **ε** and **minPts** (the desired minimum cluster size).
One way for choosing ε is by using a k-distance graph (i.e. the distance to the k = minPts-1 nearest neighbor ordered from the largest to the smallest value). Good values of ε are where this plot shows an "elbow".
Notice that if ε is too small, a large part of the points will be considered as noise, whereas if ε is too  big, the majority of objects will be clustered in the same unique cluster.

```{r,out.width="50%"}
nearest.dist=c()
dist.matrix=as.matrix(dist.matrix)
for(i in 1:ncol(dist.matrix)){
  temp=dist.matrix[,i]
  temp=temp[order(temp)]
  nearest.dist[i]=temp[3]
}
plot(1:length(nearest.dist),nearest.dist[order(nearest.dist,decreasing = TRUE)],xlab = "sample",ylab = "Distance to nearest neighbor")
abline(h=7)
```

```{r,out.width="50%"}
db=dbscan(data.var, eps = 7, minPts = 3)
p=fviz_cluster(db, data = data.var, stand = FALSE,repel=TRUE, show.clust.cent = FALSE,palette = brewer.pal(6, "Paired")[-1], ggtheme = theme_classic(),labelsize=5)
p
```

Same plot but colored by true labels

```{r,out.width="50%"}
for(i in 1:length(unique(p$data$cluster))){
  grp.i <- p$data[p$data$cluster == i, ][chull(p$data[p$data$cluster == i, c("x","y")]),]  # hull values for cluster i
  if(i==1) all_hulls=grp.i
  if(i>1) all_hulls=rbind(all_hulls,grp.i)
}

coord=as.data.frame(prcomp(data.var,scale. = TRUE)$x[,1:2])

ggplot(data = coord) + 
  geom_point(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = as.factor(labs))) +
  theme_classic()+ labs(x = p$labels$x, y = p$labels$y)+
  guides(color=guide_legend(title="Cancer type"))+
  geom_polygon(data = all_hulls, aes(x = x, y = y,group = as.factor(cluster)), alpha = 0.1)
```


**Silhouette Analysis**
```{r,out.width="50%"}
sil <- silhouette(db$cluster,dist.matrix)
fviz_silhouette(sil,palette = brewer.pal(length(unique(db$cluster)), "Paired")) + theme_classic()
```

**Adjusted Rand Index**

Since we know the true classification of the cell lines, we can compare the result of clustering to the ground truth.
We compute the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) using the R function <span style="color:blue">adjustedRandIndex()</span> contained in package "mclust".

```{r}
adjustedRandIndex(labs,db$cluster)
```


## Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM)

We now perform clustering using GMM, using the function <span style="color:blue">Mclust()</span> (package "mclust"). The parameter G indicates the number of mixture components (default is G=1:9)

```{r}
gmm <- Mclust(data.var)
summary(gmm)
```

The number of mixing components and the covariance parametrization are selected using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). BIC is a penalised (penalty for the number of estimated parameters) form of the log likelihood. We want to maximize it.

```{r,out.width="50%"}
summary(gmm$BIC)
plot(gmm, what = "BIC", legendArgs = list(x = "bottomleft"))
```

The possible models refer to different geometric characteristics of the models (volume, shape, orientation of the covariances across groups).

![](/Users/dsesia/Desktop/im1.jpg){width=50%}

**Visualization**

In order to visualize the data we want to project our data in a suitable 2-dim space. We can do that using the function <span style="color:blue">MclustDR()</span>. The directions that mostly separate the estimated clusters are recovered using the default value 1

```{r,out.width="50%"}
drgmm=MclustDR(gmm,lambda = 0.998)
# drgmm=MclustDR(gmm,lambda = 1)
```

Contour plot of estimated mixture densities
```{r,out.width="50%"}
plot(drgmm,what="contour",dimens = c(1,2))
```

Uncertainty boundaries (the uncertainty is shown using a greyscale with darker regions indicating higher uncertainty)
```{r,out.width="50%"}
plot(drgmm,what="boundaries")
```

Same plot colored by true cell type.
```{r,out.width="50%"}
ggplot(data = as.data.frame(drgmm$dir)) + 
  geom_point(aes(x = Dir1, y = Dir2, color = as.factor(labs))) +
  theme_classic()+ labs(x = "Dir1", y = "Dir2")+
  guides(color=guide_legend(title="Cell type"))
```

**Silhouette analysis**
```{r,out.width="50%"}
sil <- silhouette(gmm$classification,dist.matrix)
fviz_silhouette(sil,palette = brewer.pal(length(unique(gmm$classification)), "Paired")) + theme_classic()
```

**Adjusted Rand Index**
```{r}
adjustedRandIndex(labs,gmm$classification)
```


## Leiden

```{r,message=FALSE}
library(igraph)
```

In order to perform clustering with Leiden algorithm we first need to represent the data with a graph. In particular, starting from the distance matrix we want to construct a graph. Each node is an observation and the edges will link the most similar observations. 

How to construct an **adjacency matrix**?
For example we can consider the 5-nearest neighbors.

```{r}
n=nrow(data.var)
adj.mat=matrix(0,nrow = n,ncol=n)
colnames(adj.mat)=rownames(as.matrix(dist.matrix))
rownames(adj.mat)=rownames(as.matrix(dist.matrix))
for(i in 1:ncol(adj.mat)){
  temp=as.matrix(dist.matrix)[i,]
  temp=temp[order(temp)]
  k.nearest=names(temp)[2:6]
  adj.mat[i,which(colnames(adj.mat)%in%k.nearest)]=1
  adj.mat[which(colnames(adj.mat)%in%k.nearest),i]=1
}
colnames(adj.mat)=rownames(data.var)
rownames(adj.mat)=rownames(data.var)

adj.mat[1:5,1:5]
```

Next, we create a graph from the adjacency matrix.

```{r}
graph <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(adj.mat, mode = "undirected")
set.seed(123)
plot(graph, vertex.color = colsamples,vertex.label.cex=0.5)
legend(x="right",legend=c("COLON","LEUKEMIA","MELANOMA","NSCLC"), 
     fill=brewer.pal(4, "PiYG"),cex=0.6)
```


We now can perform Leiden clustering.
```{r}
leiden.cl=cluster_leiden(graph, objective_function = "modularity")

colcluster= brewer.pal(leiden.cl$nb_clusters, "Paired")[leiden.cl$membership]
set.seed(123)
plot(graph, vertex.color = colcluster,vertex.label.cex=0.5)
```

*Remark*: Louvain cluster can be done similarly by using the function <span style="color:blue">cluster_louvain()</span>. (Type "?cluster_louvain" for more details).

```{r,out.width="50%"}
sil <- silhouette(leiden.cl$membership,dist.matrix)
fviz_silhouette(sil,palette = brewer.pal(leiden.cl$nb_clusters, "Paired")) + theme_classic()
```
**Adjusted Rand Index**
```{r}
adjustedRandIndex(labs,leiden.cl$membership)
```


## Compare the various clustering methods using the Adjusted Rand Index

Which method performs better?

```{r,message=FALSE}
# Summary table for ARI
summ.ARI=matrix(NA,ncol = 2,nrow = 3)
colnames(summ.ARI)=c("Clustering method","ARI")
summ.ARI[,1]=c("DBSCAN","GMM","Leiden")
summ.ARI[1,2]=round(adjustedRandIndex(db$cluster, labs),3)
summ.ARI[2,2]=round(adjustedRandIndex(gmm$classification,labs),3)
summ.ARI[3,2]=round(adjustedRandIndex(leiden.cl$membership, labs),3)

knitr::kable(summ.ARI)
```
